title: Notifications on Trial
tagline: A teen and a parent put their phones' notifications and feeds on trial, auditing which alerts actually serve them and which are engineered to pull them back, then pass sentence together on what earns a place on the screen.
groupSize: Learned in class; audit done at home with a parent or guardian; verdicts shared in class
overview: A lot of screen use is not chosen; it is summoned. Notifications, autoplay, infinite feeds, streaks, and red badges are design choices meant to pull you back and keep you scrolling, and they work on adults as well as teens. This activity teaches students to see those persuasion techniques and then puts them on trial. A teen and a parent each audit their own phone: which notifications and feed features genuinely serve them (a text from a person, a calendar alert) and which are engineered hooks dressed up as helpful. Then, like a jury, they pass sentence on each one, keep, silence, or turn off, and redesign their defaults so the device serves the user instead of the other way around. The tone is balanced and empowering, not anti-technology: notifications and feeds can be genuinely useful, and the skill is telling the difference and taking back the defaults. Because parents fall for the same design, they audit alongside, making it a shared reckoning rather than a lecture.
objectives: Students will identify common engagement and persuasion techniques built into notifications and feeds.
Students will audit their own device's alerts, judging which serve the user and which serve the app.
Students will decide and justify a verdict (keep, silence, off) for each notification type.
Students will redesign their notification and feed defaults and compare the effect with a parent's audit.

print: Handout A: The Persuasion Playbook, a reference (1 per student)
Handout B: Notification Audit, worksheet (2 per student, one for the teen and one for a parent)
Handout C: The Verdict and Redesign (1 per student)
digital: Each person's own phone, to review notification and feed settings during the at-home audit
Optional: a shared note where a family records what they changed and whether it stuck

prep: Print Handout A for each student, two copies of Handout B per student (teen and parent), and one Handout C each.
Skim your own phone's notification settings so you can describe where students will look (notifications, screen-time or digital-wellbeing, feed/autoplay settings).
Set the at-home audit window and the class share day.
Add your name and the return date to the family note on Handout B.

steps.title: Who asked for this?
steps.body: Ask students to recall the last three times their phone buzzed. For each: **"Did a person reach out to you, or did an app reach out for you?"** Tally the room. Most alerts turn out to be apps, not people. Pose the trial's central question: **"Which of the things on your screen did you actually choose, and which were chosen for you to keep you coming back?"**
steps.note: The person-versus-app distinction lands fast and hard. It reframes notifications from neutral helpers to design decisions someone made for a reason.

steps.title: The persuasion playbook
steps.body: Students read Handout A, which names common techniques in plain terms: variable rewards (the slot-machine pull of maybe-something-good), red badges and counts that nag to be cleared, streaks that punish you for stopping, autoplay and infinite scroll that remove every stopping point, and "someone is active now" nudges. In pairs, students match each technique to an app they use and name what the design wants them to do. Debrief: these are not accidents; they are choices, and the same tricks work on adults.
steps.note: Keep it analytical, not preachy. Students respect being shown the mechanism and treated as capable of seeing through it, rather than being told apps are evil.

steps.title: Serve the user, or serve the app?
steps.body: Model the audit on one made-up phone. Walk through a few alerts and ask the key test for each: **"Does this serve ME (a person contacting me, a real event, something I asked for) or serve the APP (pulling me back, clearing a badge, keeping a streak)?"** Show the three possible verdicts, keep, silence (keep but no buzz or badge), or off, and model choosing one with a reason. Note that a few alerts genuinely serve the user and should stay.
steps.note: Insist on the middle verdict, silence. It prevents all-or-nothing thinking and models nuanced control: keep the information, kill the manipulation.

steps.title: The audit (at home)
steps.body: At home, the teen and a parent each run Handout B on their own phone: list their most frequent notifications and feed features, mark whether each serves the user or the app and which playbook technique it uses, and leave the verdict column for the next step. They open their actual settings together so the audit is real, not from memory. They compare: which hooks caught each of them, and were the adult's really so different?
steps.note: The parent auditing their own phone is essential; it converts a potential lecture into a shared discovery that adults are targeted too. Expect some surprise at the parent's results.

steps.title: The verdict and redesign
steps.body: Still at home, teen and parent pass sentence on Handout C: for each audited item, record keep, silence, or off with a one-line reason, then actually change the settings. They redesign defaults, turn off nonhuman badges, disable autoplay, mute streak nags, keep person-to-person and real-event alerts, and each name one feed habit to change. They note how the phone feels different and set a date to check whether the changes held.
steps.note: Push them to make the changes during the activity, not later. An audit that never touches the settings is just a worksheet; the learning is in reclaiming the defaults.

steps.title: Who's in charge now?
steps.body: Back in class, students share one notification they silenced or killed and what changed. Debrief the balanced takeaway: **"Notifications and feeds can serve you, and they're designed to serve the app. Now you can tell which is which and set your phone so you decide when to pick it up, instead of it deciding for you."**
steps.note: End on agency, not abstinence. The win is a device the student controls, not a student who feels guilty for having a phone.

unplugged: The learning runs on paper: students can read the playbook, and audit their alerts from memory, listing the notifications they get most and judging each by the serve-me-or-serve-the-app test, then write verdicts without touching a device. The analysis of persuasion design works fully unplugged.
digital: The audit is strongest with the actual phone: teen and parent open real notification, screen-time, and feed settings, see the true list, and change the defaults on the spot. This is the rare case where devices are the point, because the evidence (and the fix) lives in the settings.
whyTech: Here the digital path clearly earns its place: the manipulation and the remedy both live in the device's settings, so seeing the real alert list and actually turning hooks off produces evidence and change that a paper exercise cannot. The reading and verdicts still work unplugged for any student without a phone.

adaptations.label: Grade 9
adaptations.text: Focus on three notification types and the single serve-me-or-serve-the-app test, with keep/silence/off verdicts and no feed analysis.

adaptations.label: Higher Ed
adaptations.text: Add an ethics-and-design layer: students evaluate the incentives behind engagement design and propose what humane or regulated defaults might look like.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Provide the playbook with key terms glossed and icons for each technique; the family audit and verdicts can be done in the home language.

adaptations.label: Students without a personal phone
adaptations.text: Audit a shared or family device, or analyze screenshots the teacher provides, and still write reasoned verdicts and an ideal default design.

lookFors: Students correctly match persuasion techniques (variable rewards, badges, streaks, autoplay) to real apps.
Audits distinguish alerts that serve the user from those that serve the app, naming the technique for each.
Each verdict (keep, silence, off) carries a reason, and the student actually changed at least some defaults.
Students compare their results with a parent's and can explain that engagement design targets adults too.
reflection: Which of the things on your screen did you choose, and which were chosen for you? (Student ELE 4.1: I take responsibility for my own learning.)
How do you tell a notification that serves you from one that serves the app? (Media/AI ELE 4.1: critical thinking about designed information.)
What changed when you reset your defaults, and what did your parent's audit reveal? (Student ELE 4.3: awareness of strengths and habits.)
transfer: Families check on the review date whether the new defaults held and adjust them. In class, students carry the persuasion-design lens into analyzing feeds and recommendation systems, and connect the serve-me-or-serve-the-app test to evaluating any designed online environment.

handouts.title: The Persuasion Playbook
handouts.instructions: Read each technique. In the margin, write one app you use that does it and what the design wants you to do. These are design choices, not accidents, and they work on adults too.
paragraphs: Apps compete for your attention, and the ones that win are usually the ones best at pulling you back. Here are the most common techniques. Knowing their names makes them easier to resist.

VARIABLE REWARDS: Like a slot machine, you pull (refresh, scroll, open) and sometimes get something good, a like, a funny clip, a message, and sometimes nothing. The maybe is what hooks you; unpredictable rewards are the hardest to stop chasing.

BADGES AND COUNTS: The little red number is designed to feel like an itch you must scratch. Clearing it feels good, so you open the app, which is exactly what the badge was for. Most badges count app activity, not a real person needing you.
STREAKS: Keep a streak going for days and the app has turned stopping into a loss. You are no longer using it because you want to, but because quitting would cost you something the app invented.
AUTOPLAY AND INFINITE SCROLL: Remove every natural stopping point. The next video starts itself; the feed never ends. Without a finish line, you keep going past when you meant to stop.
SOCIAL NUDGES: "Someone is active now," "so-and-so posted," "people are waiting for your reply." These use your care about other people to pull you back on the app's schedule, not yours.

THE TEST FOR EVERY ALERT: Does this serve ME (a real person contacting me, a real event, something I actually asked for) or serve the APP (pulling me back, clearing a badge, keeping a streak)? That one question is the whole trial.

handouts.title: The Verdict and Redesign
handouts.instructions: Pass sentence on each audited item, then actually change the settings now. Keep = leave on. Silence = keep the info but no buzz or badge. Off = turn it off. Compare with your parent's results.
